beats.lead: The first true 3D shooting game was not built to be a game
beats.text: In 1973, three NASA work-study students made it while trying to solve a drier problem: how to draw a solid-looking shape on screen.
beats.note: Steve Colley had written code to hide a cube's invisible edges. Howard Palmer suggested turning it into a maze you could walk through, and by the next day Colley had one working.

beats.lead: It moved to MIT in 1974 and grew up fast
beats.text: Greg Thompson and Dave Lebling rebuilt it to run eight players at once over a shared mainframe, with text chat and a level editor.
beats.note: Players who could not book a terminal would turn up in the small hours of the morning just to get a slot.

beats.context: How many people the 1974 MIT version could put in the same maze at once, years before real time multiplayer was common on any computer.

beats.text: It spread across the young ARPANET to other universities, and reportedly got so popular that DARPA banned it at one point for eating half the traffic between MIT and Stanford.
beats.note: That claim comes from co-creator Greg Thompson's own 2004 retrospective talk, not an official DARPA record, so it is included here as a reported detail rather than a settled fact.

beats.text: Three teenagers trying to draw a better cube ended up inventing the first-person shooter.

beats.line: Before Doom, before Wolfenstein, there was a maze from a NASA work placement.
